title: Copy and Move
lead: Copy files and folders with cp, move or rename them with mv, and protect yourself from overwrite traps with -i, -n and -v.
objectives: You copy files and (with -r) folders using cp; for backups you use cp -a.
You move or rename files and folders with mv.
You think about whether the target exists and control overwriting with -i, -n and -v.

sections.title: Copying: cp
body: `cp SOURCE TARGET` creates a **copy** of the source; the source stays where it is. If the target is an existing folder, the copy goes inside it; otherwise the target becomes the new file name.

Copying folders needs **`-r`** (recursive); without it `cp` skips the folder and prints an error. If you also want to keep ownership, permissions and timestamps, use `cp -a` (archive), the safest choice for backups.

commands.what: Copies a file; the source is unchanged.
commands.where: To make a backup before editing a file or to put it elsewhere.
commands.why: If the original breaks, you still have a copy.

commands.what: Copies a folder including its contents.
commands.where: When backing up a project or photo folder.
commands.why: Without -r a folder is not copied.

commands.what: Archive copy: keeps subfolders, permissions, owner and timestamps.
commands.where: For real backups and when copying system files.
commands.why: The copy is as identical to the original as possible.

sections.tip: After copying, check both the source and the target with `ls`.

sections.title: Moving and renaming: mv
body: `mv SOURCE TARGET` **moves** a file: the source disappears and shows up at the target. Linux has no separate 'rename' command; moving within the same folder is renaming (`mv old.txt new.txt`).

Folders need no `-r`. With several sources the last argument must be an existing **folder**: `mv a.txt b.txt folder/`. Within one filesystem `mv` does not copy data, it only changes the entry, so it is very fast.

commands.what: Moves a file or folder to another folder.
commands.where: When organising files or fixing a misplaced file.
commands.why: Leaves no copy behind and takes no extra space.

commands.what: Renames in the same folder (if the target does not exist).
commands.where: To fix a file or folder name.
commands.why: Renaming = moving within the same place.

commands.what: Moves several files into a folder in one command.

sections.tip: Make sure the target folder exists before moving: if it does not, `mv a.txt folder` renames the file to `folder`!

sections.title: Overwriting and safety options
body: If a file with the same name exists at the target, `cp` and `mv` **overwrite it without asking**; the old content does not come back. This is the most common way to lose data silently.

Three safety options: **`-i`** (interactive) asks before overwriting, **`-n`** (no-clobber) leaves existing files alone, **`-v`** (verbose) prints what it does line by line. On many distributions `cp` and `mv` are aliased to `-i` for root, but not for a normal user.

commands.what: Asks for confirmation (y/n) before overwriting an existing target.
commands.where: When you are not sure whether the target exists.
In bulk copies, to protect older files.
commands.why: Quiet but safe: the target stays unchanged.

commands.what: Prints every file that is copied.
commands.where: In multi-file operations to see what happened.
commands.why: Makes it easy to verify the result.

commands.where: When moving into a folder that may hold a file with the same name.
commands.why: The file at the target is not lost.

sections.warn: `cp a b` and `mv a b` **overwrite `b` without asking** if it exists. Look with `ls b` first or add `-i` / `-n`.
sections.danger: Typing a wrong target (for example `mv notes.txt /etc/hosts`) can destroy an important system file. Take a VM snapshot before experimenting near system folders; without privileges the command simply fails.
sections.tip: For permanent safety you can define `alias cp='cp -i'` and `alias mv='mv -i'` (added to your shell configuration file).

t02.text: Make a copy of `draft.txt` called `draft_copy.txt`: `cp draft.txt draft_copy.txt`.
t02.hint: Source first, then target. Use `ls` to see both still exist.

t03.hint: Renaming is moving within the same folder; `todo.txt` must be gone.

t04.hint: It is the target of the next steps.

t05.text: Copy `draft.txt` into the `backup` folder: `cp draft.txt backup/`.
t05.hint: The trailing `/` makes clear the target is a folder.

t06.text: Copy the `photos` folder with its contents into `backup`: `cp -r photos backup/`.

t07.text: Move and rename at once: `mv draft_copy.txt backup/draft_old.txt`.
t07.hint: Giving a new name in the target renames while moving.

t08.text: Predict: what does `cp photos backup` (without `-r`) do? Run it to verify.
t08.hint: Expect an error: the folder is skipped ('-r not specified').

t09.text: Predict: what does `cat backup/draft.txt` show? Run it to verify.
t09.hint: The copy has the same content as the original: `draft v1`.

t10.text: Predict: try to move a file that does not exist: `mv ghost.txt backup`. Does it succeed?

t11.text: Debug: `report.txt` was left in the `wrong` folder by mistake. Move it to the `inbox` folder.
t11.hint: `mv wrong/report.txt inbox/`. Then check with `ls wrong inbox`.

t12.text: Mini project: create `archive/2026` with `mkdir -p`, then move `inbox/mail1.txt` there under the name `jan.txt`.
t12.hint: Two commands: `mkdir -p archive/2026`, then `mv inbox/mail1.txt archive/2026/jan.txt`.

t13.text: Challenge: rename the `photos` folder to `pictures`, then copy the `pictures` folder with its contents into `~/Documents`.
t13.hint: First `mv`, then `cp -r`; the target `~/Documents` is an existing folder.

t14.text: TICKET #2410 — Accounting wants a backup of the `inbox` folder named `backup/inbox_2026`. The original `inbox` must stay in place and complete.
t14.hint: Folder copy: `cp -r inbox backup/inbox_2026`. The target does not exist, so it becomes the new name.

t15.text: Copy with `-v` and see what happens: `cp -v tasks.txt tasks_v.txt`.
t15.hint: -v prints every copied file; verify the result with `ls`.

t16.text: Predict: `cp tasks.txt draft.txt` overwrites the target. Run it, then read the content with `cat draft.txt`. What do you see?
t16.hint: `draft v1` is gone; `buy milk` took its place. On a real system `-i` would have prevented this.

vm.intro: On your VM work in a safe folder called `~/vmlab`; never experiment with `cp` and `mv` in folders that hold real data.

v01.title: Copy a file
v01.text: Create a file, copy it and paste the `ls -l` output.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/vmlab && cd ~/vmlab
echo "original content" > original.txt
cp original.txt copy.txt
ls -l
blocks.expected:
total 8
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student 17 Jan 10 10:00 copy.txt
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student 17 Jan 10 10:00 original.txt

differs: Date, time and owner may differ; `copy.txt` and `original.txt` must appear.
The `.` mark (SELinux) appears only on Rocky/Alma, not on Ubuntu.

v02.title: Copy a folder
v02.text: Create a project folder, back it up with `cp -r` and paste the `ls -R` output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/vmlab
mkdir -p project/src
touch project/src/main.c
cp -r project project_backup
ls -R

differs: If you get `cp: -r not specified` you forgot `-r`.
The order may differ; both `project` and `project_backup` must appear.

v03.title: Move and rename
v03.text: Rename the file, then move it into a new folder and paste the result.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/vmlab
mv copy.txt renamed.txt
mkdir moved
mv renamed.txt moved/
ls . moved
blocks.expected:
.:
moved  original.txt  project  project_backup

moved:
renamed.txt

differs: If you see `mv: cannot stat` the source name is wrong; look with `ls` first.
Without creating `moved/` first, `mv renamed.txt moved/` fails.

v04.title: Prevent overwriting
v04.text: Show with `-n` that an existing file is kept. Careful: without `-n` the content would be lost.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/vmlab
echo "keep me" > keep.txt
echo "new" > other.txt
cp -n other.txt keep.txt
cat keep.txt

differs: If you see `new`, `-n` was not typed or your `cp` is very old; try `cp -i` and answer `n`.

v05.title: Clean up
v05.text: Delete the working folder. Look inside first; if no errors, press "Done".

blocks.expected: ls: cannot access '/home/student/vmlab': No such file or directory

differs: If you see `rm: cannot remove ... Is a directory`, you forgot `-r`.

q1.q: Why does `cp photos backup/` fail for a folder?
options: The folder must be renamed first
q1.explain: `cp` skips folders by default; use `cp -r` (or `cp -a`) to copy them with their contents.

q2.q: Which command renames a file within the same folder?
q2.explain: On Linux renaming is moving within the same folder: `mv old new`.

q3.q: What does `cp -i a b` do when the target already exists?
options: Ignores the target and does not copy
q3.explain: `-i` (interactive) asks for confirmation before overwriting. To never overwrite without asking, use `-n`.

q4.q: Which option best keeps permissions and timestamps when making a backup?
q4.explain: `cp -a` (archive) copies recursively and preserves permissions, owner and timestamps.

summary: `cp source target` copies, `cp -r` copies folders, `cp -a` also keeps permissions.
`mv source target` moves; in the same folder it renames, and folders need no `-r`.
If the target exists, `cp` and `mv` overwrite without asking; `-i` asks, `-n` protects, `-v` shows.
Check with `ls` whether the target exists and where things end up.

glossary.meaning: The item being copied or moved / where it goes.
Processing a folder with its subfolders and contents.
Replacing the content of a same-named target file with new content.
A recursive copy that preserves permissions, owner and timestamps.
Changing a name with mv within the same folder.
